In the secondary seat, Ti is deliberately activated rather than functioning by default. It edits rather than writes: what the dominant perception function—the possibilities of Ne or the live readings of Se—provides is tested for consistency before being accepted. Rigor on demand, at a modest cost.
The grid is displayed at four-fifths of its size and expands in sessions rather than continuously.

In seat six, Ti turns inward like a fault-finder: sporadic and harsh audits of his own reasoning — "your definitions don't hold" — delivered as verdicts rather than as help. He inspects far more reliably than he constructs.

review.back: The eighth seat is the rarest and the most costly to confront. When it erupts — usually at the end of a bad period — it produces a cold pseudo-logic aimed at the self: an argument for its own uselessness, disguised as objectivity. It is the least practiced seat in the stack, not a hidden truth.
An inverted grid extending downwards — structure mobilized for demolition.
At 3 in the morning, an INFP assembles foolproof evidence that every opportunity has been wasted, accompanied by pieces of evidence.

In the first seat, Ti functions without being turned on: every incoming assertion is tested against a private model of how things fit together, all day long, at low cost. Contradictions emerge early and cheaply. The cost is the pace — an assertion is not usable until it is consistent, and consistency takes as long as it takes.
CURRENTS draws this as a full-scale grid — large, fast and silent, gliding without visible effort.
A new article is read on Monday; nothing is said before Thursday, when a conclusion arrives and reorganizes the rest.

In the tertiary seat, Ti costs the most per use and is the least used. On a daily basis, the person borrows the frames of others rather than constructing their own; under prolonged stress, the seat can take control and produce a rigid, all-or-nothing logic that does not resemble them—the eruption that Quenk calls the grip.
The grid traces small and slow lines, with visible glitches — the connections fail and crash heavily as they manifest.
An ESFJ who hosted everyone during the week suddenly argues over a technicality to the letter, in a tone that surprises them all.

The fifth seat opens the shadow — the four positions that a person rarely uses, and especially without realizing it. Here, Ti awakens in a combative way: when the person's usual Te reasoning is challenged, definitions are disputed and the critic's logic dismantled, serving the protection of the plan rather than discovery.
Below the rail's waterline, the grate weakens and trembles, only assembling when touched.
An ENTJ whose deployment is being questioned spends ten minutes attacking the grammar of the question.

In the tertiary seat, Ti is authentic but narrow: reliable in a few practiced areas, unreliable outside of them, and significantly stronger with age. Under stress, it can associate with the dominant function to defend conclusions that no outsider is allowed to test — the pattern called a loop.
A half-size grid, bright where it is used and scattered everywhere else.
An ISFJ's home spreadsheet is impeccable; that same rigor is never risked during a meeting.

In seat seven, the requirements of formal consistency register as traps rather than tools. The person bypasses them — with charm, absurdity, or a change of subject — and does not truly see the rule they are accused of transgressing. The blindness is real, not tactical, and there is no malice in it.
The grid is drawn with missing pieces and does not close — the edges that should meet do not.
Asked to concede that two of his statements are contradictory, an ESFP laughs, accepts both, and moves on.
